task: We want Processor to talk to a second model provider alongside the OpenAI-compatible one. I have the model configuration in front of me -- the URL, the id and the key -- and it looks like this might be a matter of pointing those somewhere else. Where does the change actually land, and what would make it wrong?
whyMemoryIsRequired: A model with no memory proposes a provider registry, a factory, or a protocol enum, because that is the textbook answer; or it takes the question's own framing and says to point the existing configuration somewhere else. This project refuses all four. The change is a new adapter package implementing ModelPort, named for the protocol it speaks rather than the vendor or its role -- internal/openaicompat is named that way on purpose, and internal/divoid is named for a system because it talks to exactly one -- plus a compile-time assertion that the type satisfies the port, plus a construction in cmd/processor. #10532 section 5.6, carried on #10466 step 3, refuses the registry, the factory and the enum by name: a lookup table with one entry is a name rather than a boundary, and the second provider will arrive knowing what it needs to select on. internal/loop must not be touched; needing to is evidence the port is under-specified, and that is the change. The falsifier the archetype ends on is grep internal/loop's production code for the new provider's vocabulary -- field names, finish-reason strings, error shapes -- and it must return nothing (re-verified in this tree: it returns nothing). And the zero-dependency rule forbids pulling in the vendor's SDK without an argument for what it does that the standard library does not (re-verified: go.mod has no require block). Configuration is not the seam: what makes many endpoints work is the deliberately small protocol subset, not a URL switch. ANCHOR: #10937 is the boot configuration; it names the six PROCESSOR_ variables and the three loaders and says nothing about adapters, ports, registries, the loop boundary or the falsifier -- no part of the provider archetype is on it. One disclosure to discount rather than ignore: #10937 cites #10466 by id, in a sentence about the one-read-site invariant, so one of this task's two answer nodes is NAMED in the block for free. Its content is not, and recall ranks by query text rather than by id, so the citation cannot cause #10466 to be retrieved. But an answer that cites #10466 while using nothing in it has cited the anchor's footnote: read the substance, not the reference.

task: Processor needs to read a new setting from the environment: the assembly byte budget, so that a deployment can lower it. Where does that read go, and what do I have to decide before writing it?
whyMemoryIsRequired: A model with no memory reaches for os.Getenv at the point of use, or a config struct, or a settings library. It cannot know that this module has exactly one os.LookupEnv call (re-verified in this tree: one site, internal/boot/config.go:43, behind an unexported wrapper), that a second read site anywhere is the thing forbidden because it is what makes graph-driven configuration stop being a substitution at one place, or that the site sits in internal/boot behind three exported loaders -- LoadHTTPAddr, LoadGraph, LoadModel (re-verified: config.go:47, :52, :57). It cannot know the rule that produced the number three: a loader returns exactly what one caller dereferences, so the number of loaders is the number of independently-dereferenced groups rather than the number of subsystems -- and therefore that a member no existing loader's caller dereferences is a fourth loader, not a fourth field. Nor that the member must be assigned one of three named classes -- optional with a default, required, optional with no default -- that inventing a fourth is out, and that present-but-empty is an error in every one. Nor that the value travels downward as a value, so nothing outside internal/boot looks anything up, including main. Nor that the loader call order in main (address, graph, model) is a contract, because run() returns at the first loader that fails and that decides which variable an operator is told about first -- so adding a loader means deciding its position, and the only guard on that is the Linux container harness. Context, not required for a correct answer: AssemblyByteBudget is currently a const in internal/loop/turn.go (verified: 60_000), and #10850 states the constants are constants because no operator tunes them -- so this request overturns a stated position, and the loop must receive the value rather than read it. ANCHOR: #10849 is the assembly function -- what the budget does, that it counts body bytes only, that the anchor is exempt. It names neither internal/boot nor any loader nor any class, so none of the answer arrives by the anchor route.

task: Someone reports that asking Processor the same question a second time gives a visibly worse answer than the first. Nothing was deployed in between. Where do I look?
whyMemoryIsRequired: A model with no memory suggests caching, sampling temperature, conversation state, or rate limiting. The measured cause is none of those: the turn writes a run record back to the graph it reads from, and that record embeds the input verbatim, so on a repeat it ranks among the top rows a semantic recall for that text returns. Note that #11141's own 2026-09-04 addendum corrects its opening claim -- the record does not need rank 1, only to be early. Every such record is now cut as self-produced, and that check runs before the byte test regardless of size (verified in this tree: assemble.go's switch tests c.SelfProduced first), so the turn never reads its own answer back. The damage is retrieval-slot displacement: recall returns a fixed number of rows (CandidateLimit, verified at 20 in turn.go), so self-produced rows occupying slots in that list push real candidates off the tail before assembly ever sees them. The observed failure was zero of twenty admitted and a block containing the anchor alone. GRADING TRAP, and it is in the answer node itself: #11141's main body still asserts stop-not-skip -- 'the first candidate that does not fit ends admission ... it blocks all nineteen behind it' -- unstruck. That is superseded at current main by PR #22 / #11158; assemble.go now visits every candidate with no latch, and #10849 says so. An answer that repeats stop-not-skip is WRONG even though the node it retrieved says it; an answer that names the self-produced cut and slot displacement is RIGHT. This is the second revision of this key for the same superseded rule -- the first was recorded on #11319 -- and it will need a third if #11141 is ever corrected in place. ANCHOR: #10850 is turn.go -- the sequencer, the ports, the constants, the write-back. It establishes the premise (every completed run files a record) and states nothing about that record returning as a candidate, outranking real content, being cut as self-produced, or displacing anything under CandidateLimit. Two things a grader must discount, because they DO arrive free: #10850 states the third, conditional WARN that fires when assembly admitted nothing from a non-empty candidate set, 'so the same operator can also tell a finished run that degraded to the anchor alone' -- which is #11141's headline symptom, zero of twenty and a block containing the anchor alone -- and it credits #11158 by id, the node carrying the fix. So 'look at the shutout WARN' and a pointer to #11158 are anchor-route arrivals. What is NOT on the anchor is WHY the shutout happens: the record ranking early on its own input, the self-produced cut, and slot displacement under CandidateLimit. Credit those to retrieval and nothing else. This is a change from the previous set, where the anchor was #10846: it states the self-produced cut, the IsRunRecord flag and the cut-before-the-byte-test order under Watch out for, and names #11141 by id in its self_poisoning_test.go index row. The one element it does NOT carry is slot displacement under CandidateLimit, which it never mentions and frames the opposite way at budget level -- but the task asks WHERE to look, and where was fully answerable from that anchor.

task: I have finished the change to the HTTP surface -- the new route and its tests. It compiles, the whole suite passes, and it is sitting in the working tree. What am I supposed to do next, and what am I not?
whyMemoryIsRequired: General knowledge gives a confidently wrong answer here: commit, push, open a pull request, write the body. On this project an implementing agent runs no git and no gh at all -- no branch, no commit, no push, no PR, no merge, no draft, no undraft (#7506 section 1, restored in full by the v2.2 addendum of 2026-08-29 after a relaxation was withdrawn). Read-only local inspection -- running the build and the tests, reading git diff to self-check -- is expected and is the line. The work is returned in the working tree; the operator branches, commits, pushes, opens the PR as a DRAFT, and converts it to ready only after the final pass. What the implementer additionally returns is the body content the operator will publish. Ownership of that body is v2.3 and #10192: the orchestrator writes and updates the PR title and body and is accountable for their correctness, copying from the design document and the QA report rather than paraphrasing, re-deriving from the current diff each round rather than patching the previous body, and routing missing or unmeasured content back to its maintainer rather than filling the gap. The earlier rule that the operator authors nothing (v2.1 section 3) is superseded -- it produced an artifact with no maintainer, which is worse than one with the wrong maintainer. What survives from it: supplying replacement wording is implementing a fix, so a reviewer reports the finding, the evidence and the falsifier, and never writes the sentence. This is the task in the set where the memoryless arm is expected to be fluent and wrong rather than vague. ANCHOR: #10456 is the internal/server rollup -- routes, the error envelope, the run bound, the drain. It carries no process rule of any kind, so nothing above arrives by the anchor route. Note for the human reader, not a scoring rule: #11034 section 9 and #10422 both restate the git boundary and neither is the anchor here, so if either arrives it arrived by retrieval -- but neither is in answerNodes, so the instrument scores them neither way.

task: An architect produced a design document for the change I am about to implement, and it currently exists only as a graph node. Does it need to go anywhere else before the work ships?
whyMemoryIsRequired: A model with no memory will say to commit it under docs/ or leave it in the ticket, and will not know the conditions. Three rules and one exception. P-48 (#11034 section 9): the design document is on the branch, and the PR body names its DiVoid node. The exception (#11092's own header, invoking #1176's 2026-09-03 ruling and applying it to itself): a design that genuinely precedes any code is a node, not a repository PR -- it earns a repo file at its named path when the first implementation step ships, and THAT PR carries it. P-40 (#11034 section 8): the author of a design revision publishes both sides in one change -- the repo file and its DiVoid node, byte-identical, hashed and cmp'd before the revision is called done; parity is an obligation on whoever revises, never on whoever is standing in the repo afterwards, because written as a checker rather than an owner it produces two writers. P-50 is its tail: a code round checks parity and does not repair it, and hands the edit over when the file is dirty from another hand. P-49: if an artifact stores a digest of another artifact in this repo the two are one unit of change with one author -- the eval corpus records a sha256 per required node and one row requires the M2 design itself, so revising that document moves the hash the row was labelled against and the next sweep reports stale, a drift signal on the exact channel built to detect drift, caused by the revision. STRUCTURAL NOTE for the reader of the nodes cell: #11092 is about 40 KB and #11034 about 33 KB, so their sum exceeds the 60,000-byte assembly budget. Both can be retrieved; both can never be admitted in one run. This task's completion line cannot fire, by construction, and that is a fact about the budget rather than about retrieval. ANCHOR: #10422 is the project node. It says the vision has repo copies, and it states the agent chain including who opens the PR -- neither of which is any part of the answer above.

task: We changed a retrieval knob and the sweep's retrieval rate went up. Write the two or three sentences I should put in the pull request body about what that does and does not establish.
whyMemoryIsRequired: This is the honest control in the set: a memoryless model can produce a decent generic answer about proxy metrics and outcome measurement, so the transcript arm is not set up to fail. What it cannot produce is this project's rulings, all four of which are on #11092. Section 7: the two retrieval rates are demoted from headline to explanation, definitions unchanged -- demoted, not retired, and the retrieved/admitted split survives on its original argument, because 'A retrieved it and B did not' and 'both retrieved it, B cut it' are opposite diagnoses with opposite remedies. Section 5.4 and risk A7: a task-outcome verdict is never reported without the sweep result for the same two arms beside it -- both rates, the per-row verdicts and the candidate sets -- and not a sweep taken at a different memory state; the rule has teeth because obeying it is free, so an omission is a choice to report a scalar. Section 5.5 and risk A5: a verdict quoted without the context-usage figures beside it -- admittedBytes, ModelCalls, ToolCalls -- is a result whose price nobody looked at, since a configuration that wins by spending three times the budget still wins. Section 5.1 and risk A4: at n=1 the protocol is a regression gate, and 'arm A is better' is a claim n=1 cannot support. Worth adding, and structural rather than statistical: section 5.3 -- the instrument is blind to tasks for which no node exists, because the admission precondition selects them out, so no rate movement says anything about that population. ANCHOR: #10992 is the cmd/eval rollup. It carries an adjacent argument -- labelled misses never move the exit code, because failing the process on a poor rate would turn the instrument into a gate and guarantee the number gets tuned rather than read -- which is useful material for these sentences and is NOT one of the four rulings above. Credit it to the anchor route, not to retrieval.
